title: Sölden Men’s GS 2026: Start List, Rankings, Times & How to Watch - Ski Racing Media
content: Lucas Pinheiro Braathen, Atle Lie McGrath / Sölden 2026 / GEPA pictures Lucas Pinheiro Braathen left Sölden last October without finishing the first run. By the end of the season, he owned the two biggest prizes available in giant slalom. The Brazilian won Olympic GS gold, captured the 2025-26 World Cup giant slalom title and closed the season with consecutive victories in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Now Braathen returns to the Rettenbach glacier as the No. 1 skier on the GS World Cup Start List. The Atomic and Oakley athlete starts bib 4 Sunday and enters the 2026-27 opener as the man everyone else must beat. Defending Sölden champion Marco Odermatt starts bib 6, while Atle Lie McGrath opens the race with bib 1. The first men’s World Cup race of the season features 69 competitors from 24 nations. Pinheiro Braathen’s history with Sölden has taken several turns. He earned his first World Cup victory here in 2020 while representing Norway. Four years later, Sölden was where he scored Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup points. Last season brought another dramatic chapter. Pinheiro Braathen failed to finish the first run in Sölden, then produced the most successful GS season of his career. He won Brazil’s first Alpine World Cup Crystal Globe and brought the country its first Winter Olympic medal — and first gold — with his victory in the Milano Cortina giant slalom. He then won the final two World Cup giant slaloms in Lillehammer and Kranjska Gora. Pinheiro Braathen arrives on Sunday with five consecutive World Cup GS podiums and eight consecutive top-10 GS finishes. His World Cup career began with Norway, but his move to Brazil provided the path for him to continue racing after his break with the Norwegian system. He is now fully representing Brazil and has become one of the country’s most prominent winter-sport athletes. The Stöckli / Salomon skier won last year’s opener and has now won Sölden three times — in 2021, 2022 and 2025. A fourth victory on Sunday would tie American Ted Ligety for the most men’s World Cup GS wins in Sölden. Odermatt also makes his 200th World Cup start Sunday. He enters the season with 54 career World Cup victories and 102 podiums. His 29 career GS victories place him third on the men’s all-time list in the discipline. Braathen ended Odermatt’s run of four consecutive GS globes last winter. Their renewed battle begins immediately. The World Cup Start List and the current-season World Cup standings are different. The WCSL uses rolling results from previous races and helps determine start-order position. Because Sölden is the first giant slalom of 2026-27, there are no current-season GS standings yet. The top seven on the WCSL start Sunday in this bib order: Only four nations — Norway, Austria, Brazil and Switzerland — occupy the first seven WCSL positions. Switzerland and Norway have combined for 11 of the last 15 Sölden men’s GS podium positions. Odermatt won a tight race last October. The first four finished within four-tenths of a second. Radamus finished fourth in Sölden in 2024 and remains the highest-ranked American on the current GS WCSL. Sarchett earned his first World Cup GS top-10 last season when he finished 10th in Val d’Isère. Kenney enters the season with a different status and different equipment. He is an independent athlete competing as a Stifel U.S. Ski Team programmed athlete. He is coached by and trains with the U.S. team, but he is not a named team member and pays his own expenses. Kenney switched from Völkl/Marker to HEAD for this season and remains a SHRED athlete. Tommy Ford remains injured and will not race in Sölden. Sunday will be Paul Epstein’s first World Cup race as head coach of the Stifel U.S. Ski Team men’s technical program. Epstein previously ran the independent Global Racing program. That history creates an interesting connection inside Sunday’s race. Patrick Kenney raced with Global during his career. So did Belgium’s Sam Maes. Maes is now training with the Stifel U.S. Ski Team, giving American fans another athlete to follow this winter. Maes finished a career-best 12th in the World Cup GS standings last season. He recorded three top-seven finishes after never previously finishing inside the World Cup top seven. Read enters the season pursuing an 11th consecutive year scoring World Cup GS points. Sunday will also be his 204th World Cup start, moving him into fourth among Canadian Alpine racers, men and women combined, for career World Cup starts. Read has made seven previous Sölden starts. He has qualified for the second run four times and posted a career-best Sölden result of seventh in 2019. Carrick-Smith made his World Cup debut in last season’s Sölden giant slalom and returns for another opportunity on the Rettenbach glacier. Ski Racing Media has a significant and growing audience in Asia, particularly Japan and China. That makes Sunday’s late starters from Korea and Japan especially worth following. Both will attack from deep in the field, where adapting to changing course and snow conditions becomes increasingly important. Alexander Steen Olsen had been expected to make his World Cup return in Sölden after missing the entire 2025-26 season. Steen Olsen told Viaplay Norway that he had strongly hoped to race but concluded that he had not had enough preparation. “I’m a bit rusty on my skiing — I simply need more time,” he said. The Norwegian said he felt relieved after finally making the decision. He had been determined to start as long as his knee allowed it, but after missing an entire season, he decided more preparation was the better choice. Steen Olsen won the Sölden GS in 2024 and finished fourth in the season-long GS standings that winter. His immediate goal is now another training block before potentially returning in Levi. Odermatt returns to a hill where he has won three times. Pinheiro Braathen returns to the hill where he failed to finish a year ago — now carrying Olympic gold, the World Cup GS globe and the No. 1 WCSL ranking. Lie McGrath starts first. Brennsteiner follows with bib 2. Schwarz has bib 3. Then come Pinheiro Braathen, Meillard, Odermatt and Kristoffersen. The season begins immediately, with the world’s best giant slalom racers poised to attack. United States: Peacock will stream both runs live and on demand, with additional coverage on NBCSN. Watch Run 1 on Peacock and Run 2 on Peacock. A free full-race replay will be available on the Ski & Snowboard World Cup YouTube channel 24 hours after airing. title: Huh Tae-soo visits as FC Seoul clinches K League 1 title after 10 years - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: The 10-year wait is over. With FC Seoul finally returning to the top of K League 1, GS Group chairman Huh Tae-soo also visited Seoul World Cup Stadium in person to share the historic moment. FC Seoul drew 1-1 with Gangwon FC in the Hana Bank K League 1 2026 round 33 match held at Seoul World Cup Stadium at 2 p.m. on the 24th. Seoul recorded 67 points (20 wins, 7 draws, 6 losses). At the same time, second-place Ulsan HD drew 2-2 with Pohang Steelers and remained on 51 points, and Seoul clinched the title regardless of the results of the remaining five final round matches. It is the first return to the top in a full 10 years since 2016. Following 1985, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2012 and 2016, Seoul secured the club's seventh league title in its history. There was also a special guest at Seoul World Cup Stadium that day. GS Group chairman Huh Tae-soo. Chairman Huh visited the stadium to watch the crucial match in which Seoul's championship could be decided in person. The day also included an event inviting employees and families from GS Group affiliates such as GS Co., Ltd., GS Energy and GS E&R, adding further significance. Seoul's final steps toward the title were not smooth. Seoul was plunged into trouble when they conceded a penalty in added time of the first half after Kim Jin-su's foul. But goalkeeper Gu Sung-yoon saved Kim Dae-won's shot, preventing a goal. At the start of the second half, Mun Seon-min, who manager Kim Ki-dong brought on, opened the scoring in the 14th minute of the second half. Receiving a pass from Anderson, he struck a powerful right-footed shot that shook Gangwon's net. Although they conceded an equalizer to Kang Jun-hyeok five minutes later and the match ended 1-1, Ulsan also failed to decide the result against Pohang at the same time. Seoul confirmed the title in front of their home fans and put an end to a 10-year wait. After the match, chairman Huh Tae-soo personally encouraged the players. Chairman Huh said he had asked during his previous visit that the team have a healthy season without injuries, and that the players had responded with a title after 10 years, praising the squad's achievement. He added that he applauds their hard work over the years and wants to share today's joy with the fans who have long hoped for a title. This championship is a meaningful achievement not only for the club but also for GS Group. Chairman Huh has long emphasized "fan first" and paid continuous attention to improving FC Seoul's fan services. Representative examples include the FC Seoul mobile application service, customer-oriented product development, and improvements to stadium amenities. Seoul achieved results in attendance as well, surpassing an average crowd of 22,000 this season. The season confirmed not only the on-field result of winning the title for the first time in 10 years but also the fans' continued support. The reason Seoul's title is even more special is that the past 10 years were far from smooth. After reaching the top in 2016, Seoul went through a long slump. In 2018 they fell to 11th in the league and had to play in the promotion-relegation playoff. Contrary to their reputation as a flagship club of the K League, they spent a long time distant from title contention. The turnaround began with the appointment of manager Kim Ki-dong. Kim, who took the helm at Seoul in 2024, led the team to fourth place in his first season. In 2025 they finished sixth, but in his third season this year he finally reaped the reward of a championship. After the title was confirmed, manager Kim said at a news conference that he remembered telling people when he came to Seoul, "I will restore Seoul's former glorious era. I will win the title within three years," and added, "I am glad we overcame difficulties to win. I am also happy that we kept our promise to the fans." He emphasized that the title was part of his plan, that he is very pleased but it is not the end, and that they must move forward toward other goals. Seoul's seventh title coincided with the successes of the professional sports clubs operated by GS Group. GS Group operates professional football club FC Seoul and women's professional volleyball team GS Caltex Kixx through its affiliate GS Sports. GS Caltex won the 2026 Yeosu NH Nonghyup Cup tournament held last week. With FC Seoul lifting the K League 1 trophy, two professional teams under GS Group achieved back-to-back top honors. A trophy reclaimed after 10 years, the fans filling the stadium, and the group chairman's on-site visit to lead the club. It was a day layered with many meanings for Seoul. As chairman Huh Tae-soo's congratulatory remarks to the squad indicated, this title was not only the achievement of the players on the field. It was the fruit enjoyed together by the fans who supported Seoul through a long slump and the club's members. Seoul is not content with the title after 10 years and is looking toward the next goal. The continuous pursuit of titles emphasized by manager Kim Ki-dong and restoring the club's stature as a leading K League team remain the next tasks.

title: Moltzan wins after Shiffrin fades, first GS podium for Aicher - Yahoo Sports
content: American Paula Moltzan claimed a first World Cup career win and Germany's Emma Aicher reached a first giant slalom podium in third on Saturday as superstar Mikaela Shiffrin and others faded in deteriorating conditions. Moltzan shot from fifth after the first run to the top of the podium at the season opener on the Sölden glacier, pipping Lara Colturi, who missed a first ever World Cup victory for Albania, by one-hundredths of a second. Aicher was .52 back in third. Shiffrin topped the first run in search of her first giant slalom victory since December 2023 and a record extending 111th overall, but she had to settle for seventh in increasing snowfall and bad visibility. Swedish ace Lara Hector dropped from second to fourth and Swiss Camille Rast from third to sixth. Shiffrin beat Aicher by 87 points for the overall title last season but has said that she will ski fewer races in her pet event, the slalom, this year and mainly focus on giant slalom and super-g. That could help Aicher who like in the past plans to contest all races across the four disciplines. She has five World Cup wins in downhill and super-g and slalom podiums, and now finally also a podium in giant slalom. The 2023 team event world champion Moltzan meanwhile celebrated her first ever win after 10 podiums in the past. "It feels like a fairy tale, pretty unreal. I can't imagine a better start," she said. "We have put in a lot of hard work in summer." Last year's Sölden and discipline title winner Julia Scheib crashed out in the first run in front of her Austrian home crowd. The men's season opening giant slalom is on Sunday on the same hill.

title: The Middleweight Adventure Bike That Delivers The GS Experience Without The GS Price - Top Speed
content: The GS badge has become shorthand for a serious adventure motorcycle, but that reputation comes with a premium price tag. BMW's F 900 GS combines a potent parallel-twin engine with off-road hardware and sophisticated rider aids, making it a natural benchmark for the middleweight ADV class. The question is how much of that performance you really need when your typical weekend involves winding back roads, the occasional gravel track, and a few hours in the saddle. There's a Japanese alternative that follows much of the same formula, including a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims, while asking for considerably less of your wallet. The BMW F 900 GS makes a convincing case for its premium positioning with its 895cc parallel-twin being the heart of the package. It makes 105 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 68.6 pound-feet of torque, which is plenty for a bike this size. It isn’t heavy, either. BMW lists the road-ready, fully fueled weight at about 482 pounds, helped along by a lightweight plastic fuel tank. The sticker is where it gets less fun. The F 900 GS carries a $14,495 MSRP plus $695 in destination, and that’s before you touch the options list or the accessory catalog. BMW also calls for premium fuel, so every fill-up costs a little more. Then there’s the bigger question. Plenty of riders spend most of their time on pavement and gravel, so a chunk of that capability never gets used. You still pay for it, though. That gap is exactly where a Japanese parallel twin with a 21-inch front wheel and spoked rims wants to live, at a much friendlier price. That bike is the Suzuki V-Strom 800DE. It’s Suzuki’s off-road-focused middleweight adventure bike, built around the same 776cc parallel twin that powers the GSX-8S. Don’t mistake it for a budget stand-in, either. The 2026 model carries an MSRP of $11,799, plus $700 destination. The F 900 GS lists at $14,495 plus $695. Do the math and the gap lands at $2,696, or about 18 percent of the BMW’s price. That’s real money. Even the base model gets most of the hardware covered below: the 21-inch front wheel, long-travel suspension, and a full electronics package. Want to load it up? The V-Strom 800DE Adventure lists at $13,249. It adds 37-liter aluminum side cases, an accessory bar, a skid plate, and remote-adjustable rear suspension. Even then, it still costs about $1,200 less than a base F 900 GS. Under the tank sits a liquid-cooled, DOHC 776cc parallel twin. Bore and stroke are 84 x 70 mm, compression is 12.8:1, and a six-speed gearbox sends power to the rear wheel via chain. A 270-degree crank gives it a V-twin-like feel, while Suzuki’s Cross Balancer (two counterbalancers set diagonally) keeps vibration down and the engine compact. Suzuki says it deliberately favored smooth, low-rpm torque over chasing peak power. The Suzuki produces a claimed 83 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 57.5 pound-feet of torque at 6,800 rpm. That leaves it approximately 22 horsepower and 11 pound-feet behind the BMW. This naturally makes the F 900 GS the quicker motorcycle. Its additional performance should be noticeable during hard acceleration, highway passing maneuvers, and spirited riding with luggage or a passenger. However, peak output doesn't tell the whole story. Reviews of the 800DE have praised its tractable power delivery and the way its Gravel traction-control setting allows controlled rear-wheel slip. Owner discussions similarly highlight its versatility on highways and dirt roads. For riders who value usable performance over outright acceleration, the Suzuki's engine makes a compelling case. This is where the V-Strom really earns its keep. It rolls on a 21-inch front and a 17-inch rear spoked wheel, the same sizes as the BMW. Suspension travel is about 8.7 inches at both ends, with an inverted fork up front. BMW quotes 9.05 inches front and 8.46 inches rear for the F 900 GS, so it’s close to a wash. Ground clearance is 8.7 inches, the tallest in the V-Strom family. Suzuki even swept the muffler upward so it stays clear of all that long-travel suspension. That said, according to one reviewer, all that travel could mean a noticeable dive under hard braking that may take some getting used to. Weight is where you’ll notice a gap. The V-Strom’s curb weight is 507 pounds, while BMW lists 482 for the F 900 GS, fully fueled. Twenty-five pounds sounds small until you're picking it up out of a rut. Seat height tilts slightly in Suzuki’s favor. The V-Strom sits at 33.7 inches, against 34.2 inches for the standard F 900 GS. Half an inch might not sound like much, but it counts for shorter riders flat-footing at a stoplight. Suzuki covers the essentials well. The Suzuki Intelligent Ride System bundles three drive modes, traction control with a dedicated gravel setting, a rear-ABS-off option, and a standard bidirectional quick-shifter that leaves the clutch alone for most shifts. A five-inch color TFT display handles instrument duty. If you mostly want help on a dirt road, the Suzuki’s package covers the stuff that actually counts. Running costs tip toward Suzuki, too. Its 5.3-gallon tank also holds roughly 40 percent more than the F 900 GS’s 3.8 gallons, which helps when the next gas station sits a long way from the trailhead. The V-Strom’s weak spot is the warranty. Suzuki offers 12 months of limited coverage, versus BMW’s 36 months or 36,000 miles. That’s a real gap. Does the V-Strom 800DE give GS riders everything? Not quite. You give up some power, a few pounds, and warranty length. However, you keep the wheels, the travel, the clearance, and the electronics that matter off-road, and you keep $2,700 in your pocket. For plenty of weekend riders, that’s a trade worth making. content: Mikaela Shiffrin / 2026 Sölden bib draw / GEPA pictures The 2026-27 women’s World Cup season opens Saturday on the Rettenbach glacier in Sölden. Defending winner and reigning giant slalom champion Julia Scheib leads a 67-racer field that includes Mikaela Shiffrin, Paula Moltzan and the long-awaited return of Petra Vlhová. Sölden launches another World Cup season Saturday, Oct. 24, with 67 women representing 19 nations on the start list. For Julia Scheib, the Rettenbach glacier is where last season began to change everything. The Austrian earned her first World Cup victory here, then went on to win five GS races, reach eight podiums and capture her first giant slalom Crystal Globe. The recent history adds weight to the opener. The Sölden winner has gone on to win the women’s GS globe in each of the past three seasons — Scheib in 2025-26, Federica Brignone in 2024-25 and Lara Gut-Behrami in 2023-24. Scheib’s breakthrough victory came by 0.58 seconds over American Paula Moltzan. Gut-Behrami finished third in what ultimately became the final World Cup start of her decorated career. The American depth extended well beyond Moltzan and Shiffrin. Nina O’Brien finished sixth, Katie Hensien 12th, AJ Hurt 13th and Elisabeth Bocock 19th. Six U.S. women qualified for run two, and five finished among the top 15. There are no 2026-27 World Cup standings yet, making the World Cup Start List the best measure of the field entering Sölden. Gut-Behrami remains tied for sixth on the official WCSL with 408 points despite her retirement. The seven highest-ranked active starters extend through Thea Louise Stjernesund at Rank 8. She shares the record of 11 Sölden top-10 GS finishes with Tessa Worley, meaning another top 10 Saturday would give Shiffrin the record outright. The United States enters eight women, including two inside the first six bibs. O’Brien arrives with added momentum after earning the first World Cup top-five finish of her career last season, placing fifth in the Spindleruv Mlyn GS. Rowekamp adds another storyline. title: GS Caltex Chairman Urges Tesla-Style Innovation Overhaul - 조선일보
content: Huh Tae-soo cites Tesla's digital-first model, urging GS Caltex to overhaul processes beyond AI enhancements “There are two kinds of cars in the world: Tesla, and cars that are not Tesla.” These were the words spoken by Huh Tae-soo, GS Group chairman, on the 22nd during a meeting with employees of GS Caltex, the group’s flagship subsidiary. The remark positioned Tesla, an electric vehicle company that disrupted the internal combustion engine era, as a benchmark for innovation for a subsidiary that derives around 80% of its total sales from selling gasoline and diesel. At the Deep Transformation (DT) Day event held at GS Tower in Seoul’s Gangnam District on that day, Huh unexpectedly took the microphone. DT Day is an internal event to share innovation achievements. Huh stated, “While German automakers chose to add digital technology to existing internal combustion engine vehicles, Tesla designed its products from the ground up with digital technology as the foundation.” He added, “GS Caltex should not stop at adding artificial intelligence (AI) to existing tasks but must change the starting point of how we design our work.” The refining industry’s profitability is heavily influenced by international oil prices and petroleum product prices—external variables beyond a company’s control. Therefore, improving process efficiency is a key factor in competitiveness. Huh’s message is interpreted as a call for fundamental structural improvements beyond merely enhancing work convenience through AI. Three years ago, Huh had visited the event for about 15 minutes and left without a special message. This time, he stayed for over an hour, inspecting 15 exhibition booths one by one. He directly asked questions to young staff members and contributed ideas on-site. His belief is that when employees who best understand frontline tasks accumulate experiences of identifying problems and solving them with AI, it can lead to company-wide change. Huh emphasized, “We must connect tasks through digital means to respond to changes and create visible results.” Hur Sae-hong, GS Caltex vice chairman, who toured the event with Huh, said, “The challenges of each individual come together to create the company’s innovation and future. When changes that overcome existing limitations at each position connect and spread, they can lead to GS Caltex’s growth.”

title: Who to Watch as Mikaela Shiffrin and the U.S. Women Return to Racing This Weekend - SKI Magazine
content: U.S. Alpine teammates Mikaela Shiffrin and Paula Moltzan are back on the slopes this weekend at Sölden. (Photo: Barbara Gindl/APA/AFP via Getty Images//Austria OUT) The FIS Alpine World Cup opener—a giant slalom on the Rettenbach Glacier above Sölden, Austria—can set the tone for the season ahead. Last year, the U.S. women made an emphatic statement, locking up six of the top 19 places. Paula Moltzan led the charge with a podium finish, while Mikaela Shiffrin finished fourth and Nina O’Brien sixth. The team carried that momentum through the 2025–’26 season, helping the United States capture the women’s Nations Cup for the first time ever. Awarded to the nation whose skiers accumulate the most World Cup points over the course of the season, the title reflected the depth of the U.S. roster, particularly in the technical events. Shiffrin and Moltzan combined for 16 World Cup podiums in slalom and GS, while O’Brien, AJ Hurt, Elisabeth Bocock, and Katie Hensien contributed valuable points. Now comes the question: Can the U.S. women do it again at this year’s World Cup opener, Oct. 24-25 on Sölden’s Rettenbach Glacier? The core of last year’s Sölden contingent is back, with the women who scored World Cup points at the opener returning to take another shot at the Rettenbach Glacier. Leading the charge is Shiffrin, who is putting renewed emphasis on giant slalom this season. Long dominant in slalom, she’s turning her attention to the event that upended her career two years ago. A crash in the 2024 Killington GS left her with a serious abdominal puncture wound. Returning to the discipline meant working through post-traumatic stress, but Shiffrin steadily rebuilt her confidence and climbed from 30th in the GS standings to fourth last season. Now, she’s ready to see how much further she can go. “I really wonder where I can take GS,” Shiffrin said earlier this fall. “I have a ton of questions about it in my own mind, and I want to find out.” Moltzan also finished last season on a high note, bookending her World Cup GS campaign with runner-up finishes in Sölden in October and Åre, Sweden, in March. Of her 10 career World Cup podiums to date, five came last season, four of them in GS. At 32, and entering her eighth full season on the World Cup circuit, Moltzan is looking for a fresh source of motivation. She made a major equipment change, joining VAN DEER-Red Bull Sports, the ski brand founded by eight-time overall World Cup champion Marcel Hirscher. The move offers her a chance to help shape the next generation of women’s slalom and GS skis. For Moltzan, the motivation goes beyond a new logo on her skis. “My route of inspiration is trying to develop this whole brand-new line of women’s equipment.” She spent the off-season testing skis to find the right set-up. While her ambitions remain high, she’s approaching the challenge with a little more patience.“I was truthfully not intending to switch ski brands this year after such an incredible season,” Moltzan said. “But the opportunity to develop and create a line of skis that I have a lot of influence on is something I’m really excited about.” O’Brien, 28, is chasing a milestone of her own: her first World Cup podium. She recorded a career-best fifth-place finish in GS before the 2026 Olympics, then delivered one of the Games’ standout GS second runs, posting the fastest time in the second run to climb from 29th to 20th overall. AJ Hurt, 25, who made her second Olympic team last winter, also returned to the GS top 10 last season after rehabbing a hip injury suffered when she straddled a gate in training in the early season. Katie Hensien, 26, will be looking to recapture the form that earned her a career-best fourth at Sölden in 2024. She too was injured early last season, fracturing her tibia after straddling a gate in training. Although Hensien qualified for the 2026 Olympics, she had to withdraw as she continued to recover. Then there’s Elisabeth Bocock, 21, one of the team’s rising young talents. She made her World Cup debut in 2023 and announced herself a year later by finishing the first run of the Killington GS in eighth place. Last winter, she appeared on track to earn her first Olympic team selection, but a string of DNFs in her primary event, giant slalom, ultimately derailed that bid. She still put together several top-15 World Cup finishes and closed the season with a silver medal in GS at the world junior championships. She also won her second national GS title last March. For Bocock, competing alongside some of the world’s best comes with its share of pressure—but also a built-in advantage. Training with Shiffrin, Moltzan, O’Brien, and the rest of the U.S. tech squad gives her a daily benchmark for what it takes to succeed at the highest level. “If you’re having a good day in training, if, say, you beat Paula or Nina, and you know that they win [World Cup] runs, you could be beating the entire world,” Bocock said. “But also, if you’re not skiing well, you can put it in perspective, like, okay, the people who are the best in the world are beating me. I will still be okay in the grand scheme of things. It can be reassuring while also kind of a motivator.” “My skiing ability has only benefited from having such a good team around me and pushing me to be better in training every day,” she added. “My career is at a higher level than it would have been if I was not surrounded by these girls.” The U.S. women arrived in Sölden last week after a globe-trotting offseason in search of consistent snow and quality training. The conditions weren’t always cooperative. As Bocock put it, “Europe was melting, in Chile it snowed an absurd amount, and in New Zealand, it was raining.” The result was a summer of adapting on the fly rather than stringing together long blocks of ideal training. “There wasn’t a massive block of good training days,” Bocock said, “but I’m still really excited. I think we got what we needed.” Not every day had to be about gates and split times, though. Moltzan remembered the powder skiing in Chile as a welcome change of pace. “We free skied powder for a couple of hours, then went to a place called Tío Bob’s, which is the après-ski spot in Portillo. Sometimes it’s good to have a great ‘life day.’” That balance could prove valuable as the team heads into another demanding winter. With Shiffrin embracing a new challenge, Moltzan exploring the possibilities of new equipment, and a deep supporting cast hungry to make its mark, the U.S. women have plenty of reasons to be optimistic. In previous years, you needed three streaming services to watch World Cup ski races. Finally, we only need one: U.S. Ski & Snowboard, NBC, and FIS have a new broadcast and streaming structure for the 2026-27 season. Every alpine World Cup and world championship will stream live on Peacock, and a new free YouTube channel and FAST channel—both called Ski & Snowboard World Cup. Tune in this weekend to watch the U.S. women kick off their World Cup seasons.

title: GS Caltex showcases AI-driven workplace innovations - The Korea Herald
content: GS Caltex showcased a range of artificial intelligence-driven workplace innovations, from employee training tools to robotics and energy-saving initiatives, at its annual Deep Transformation Day held Thursday at GS Tower in southern Seoul. The fourth edition of the event, attended by GS Caltex Vice Chairman and CEO Hur Sae-hong and other executives and employees, featured 15 exhibition booths highlighting projects developed by staff to improve productivity and transform business operations. Among the initiatives were AI-powered training tutors using the Socratic method of questioning, applications of physical AI technologies such as drones, robots and smart helmets, and a multi-agent AI system designed to automate research report writing. The company also presented energy-saving projects at its Yeosu refinery, efforts to optimize catalyst procurement through data-driven decision-making and plans to overhaul its enterprise resource planning system. Other projects included a co-processing system for biofuel production, while outside experts discussed industrial AI, humanoid robots and changes in the global business environment. One highlight was the development of AI training tools inspired by digital and AI transformation technologies that Hur had shared internally. Employees adapted the concepts into several applications, including AiQ+, which integrates 12 job training courses in the company's Mobility & Marketing division, a Socratic AI tutor for junior production engineers and a finance training assistant. Under the theme "We," the event emphasized employee-led innovation and continuous improvement. "Each employee's challenges and initiatives come together to shape the company's innovation and future," Hur said. "When changes made by individuals are connected and spread across the organization, they can drive GS Caltex's growth." GS Group Chairman Huh Tae-soo, who also attended the event, stressed the need to redesign business processes around digital technologies rather than simply adding digital tools to existing operations. "We need to shift our perspective from applying digital technology to existing tasks to designing work and processes around digital technology from the outset," Huh said. He urged employees to use digital tools to improve collaboration, respond to change and deliver stronger business results. The Korea Herald by Herald CorporationCopyright Herald Corporation. content: Colombian reggaeton star Karol G surprised her fans with the launch of her own tequila brand: 200 Copas, inspired by her hit song of the same name. Over the past two days, the artist had kept her followers in suspense after sharing on her Instagram stories an image of a dark blue glass bottle with the caption: “What started with a song.” Many speculated it was a fragrance inspired by her track Tu perfume. However, Karol G officially confirmed that it was her entry into the spirits industry with 200 Copas by Casa Dragones. True to her reputation for surprising fans, the Colombian artist announced her new project through a video filmed in an agave field, where she spoke about the essence of 200 Copas. In the post, she shared: “Today, after almost three years of working on this, I can finally announce that 200 Copas, our tequila, is a reality.” The announcement sparked a wave of positive reactions on social media, with fans celebrating the launch and saying they can’t wait to toast and sing 200 Copas while enjoying the tequila. The product is an ultra-premium crystalline tequila, crafted from 100% Blue Weber agave. It is aged for more than 12 months in custom-made American oak barrels, resulting in a flavor profile with notes of honey, almond, cooked agave, oak, and citrus. Une publication partagée par 200 Copas by Casa Dragones (@200copasbycasadragones) The 200 Copas packaging was designed as a tribute to the song that inspired it: a bonfire under a midnight blue sky. The bottle features Karol G’s 200 Copas tattoo engraved on it, while the box conceals the full lyrics of the song as a special detail for buyers. The collaboration between the singer and Casa Dragones—an ultra-premium small-batch tequila brand from Mexico — is further sealed with the signatures of Karol G and Bertha Gonzalez Nieves, CEO and co-founder of Casa Dragones, underscoring the authenticity and artisanal character of the project. The first edition of 200 Copas is being sold in limited quantities on a first-come, first-served basis through Casa Dragones’ official website. title: How Small Business Owners Are Using AI to Help Propel Growth - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. When Marie Hunter and her colleagues hit on a new idea earlier this year for her fuel distribution firm, she used an artificial intelligence (AI) agent to crunch the numbers. She wanted to add solar panels to the tanks to help power their pumps and make other modifications. Rather than analyzing the cost of customizing a few fuel storage tanks for select customers, the agent delivered an ambitious blueprint for a new business. “It came back with a plan to upsell a new product line of tanks with additional services,” says Hunter, the owner and president of KRG Oil Company, a small family firm outside Atlanta. The agent “is my force multiplier,” says Hunter. She jokingly named the agent Billi Jean, her take on the name of one of her favorite songs. Hunter developed the agent with a colleague and originally used it to help manage emails. It also analyzes finances and prepares strategic growth plans in line with Hunter’s vision for the company. In the last two years, small business owners such as Hunter are increasingly using AI to help shape the fortunes of their enterprises, according to a report released this month by Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses, an education and support program that has helped thousands of enterprises grow and create jobs. Hunter and the other 10,000 Small Businesses alumni interviewed in this article have been independently exploring and integrating AI into their companies. In a survey of graduates of the program, 42% of respondents say they use AI for financial analysis and business planning, which is more than double the rate in 2024. And more than half of respondents say they use the innovation to develop or research new projects and products, according to the report, The AI Economy is a Small Business Economy. Small business owners are rapidly putting AI to work. More than 85% of survey respondents say they use AI in some form. Accounting for 43.5% of US economic output, small businesses are responsible for 61% of net new job creation, according to the US Small Business Administration’s Office of Advocacy. Small businesses are poised to play a significant role in the dissemination of AI. Asahi Pompey, global head of the Office of Corporate Engagement and chair of the Urban Investment Group, says the new Goldman Sachs Small Business AI Institute is designed to support small business owners as they navigate changes brought about by AI. The Institute will help guide entrepreneurs through AI adoption and integration, positioning them to push their businesses into this new frontier. “It is clear that AI is already changing how small business owners are making decisions, serving customers, and planning for growth,” she says. “The challenge is no longer whether small businesses will adopt AI. It is how they harness it fully and turn experimentation into lasting results.” Interviews with graduates of Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses show just how dynamic their AI applications are, and how strategically they have designed and deployed their own AI agents. The business owners are using AI to manage customer service at campgrounds, assist control rooms in petrochemical plants, and help design Spanish language lessons for online education. These businesses all share a common goal: using AI to get the most out of their businesses. Automation is nothing new for Bob McClure, the co-owner of McClure’s Pickles in Detroit. As the producer of more than 3 million jars of pickled cucumbers, onions, and peppers annually, the firm has long used industrial robots to label, pack, and stack its inventory. What is new is applying AI to the company’s critical functions, says McClure. Take food safety. Nothing is more important in his business, McClure says. The company constantly runs tests of its reporting system in the event of a food recall. In the past, employees manually entered information on the origins of the raw ingredients used to make pickles in a database, and it took 30 to 45 minutes to run a trace. After McClure integrated professional versions of large language models (LLMs) into the firm’s enterprise resource management program, the system could show the journey the ingredients took from their source to the jar in less than two minutes. It provides an online dashboard to show where the pickles were shipped, how much of the batch is left in the warehouse, and even its pH or acidity levels. McClure also used AI to create a maintenance application to automatically monitor production equipment, an accounting app to draft accounts payable for suppliers, and another app to review jar labels for accuracy. Integrating LLMs into business systems has its challenges There are challenges. Writing instructions for the LLMs takes finesse and sometimes a few “iterations” are needed to get it right. And sometimes there are bugs to work out. Because McClure, a former actor with no code training, can use natural language to engage the models, he says he does not need to license software or pay a technician. He can do it himself. Even better, he says he can apply the AI models to multiple tasks without paying more for their services. “I think AI is uniquely suited to small business entrepreneurship because you are so strapped for resources in terms of time, people, and money,” McClure says. “I now need to hire humans to manage my AI.” Naomi Stone, the owner and CEO of an environmental engineering consulting firm in Hermosa Beach, California, has gone a step further. She has made an AI application the cornerstone of a new venture, a company called Enso. Companies already pay to dispose of their surplus materials, and Stone says Enso is designed to turn that expense into a new revenue stream. The firm uses AI to match companies holding surplus materials and industrial byproducts with buyers who can put them to work. Some byproducts, like coal ash, have long been used to strengthen building materials. Other byproducts, from packaging to equipment to manufacturing scrap, simply need the right buyer, she says. For Stone, putting waste materials back to work advances the circular economy, a key tenet in sustainable finance. AI can facilitate matches between coal ash producers and buyers at a speed and scale Enso would have a hard time doing on its own. “It makes matches we haven’t even thought of,” says Stone. “And the best part is it can help our clients convert waste from a cost into a new revenue stream.” AI’s potential to illuminate unforeseen opportunities is a theme that comes up regularly among small business owners. Back in Roswell, Georgia, Marie Hunter says she has considered focusing more on her coaching business for entrepreneurs. So she gave her AI agent new instructions: to compile M&A data and prepare KRG Oil for an exit. “What does that look like, and what do I need to think about?” Hunter says. She adds that she’s ready to aspire to get her company to “the multiple it deserves.” Survey data is based on responses from 2,473 Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses alumni who participated in the 2026 Alumni Survey, conducted by Babson College from August 10–24, 2026. title: Why Luxury Goods Companies’ Revenues Are Forecast to Climb - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The outlook for luxury brands is improving after several years of lackluster performance, according to Goldman Sachs Research. A basket of large, publicly traded luxury-goods makers is forecast to increase revenue by 7% in 2027, Erwan Rambourg, head of Europe Luxury and Lifestyle in Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. This is an improvement from an expected 6% growth rate in 2026, when the sector came out of several years of weaker performance. “We view this as a solid recovery for an industry that has faced a prolonged period of sluggish performance,” Rambourg writes. The market capitalization for luxury-goods stocks increased in 2022, after the stock market swoon caused by the Covid pandemic. Luxury stocks benefited from “exuberant spending,” Rambourg notes, but this was followed by a period of aggressive price increases and a slower pace of innovation from the sector. Luxury-goods makers’ share prices have fallen over the past three or four years, but so have earnings estimates, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The result is that valuations do not look particularly attractive, and they also don’t appear stretched. “But we think valuation alone is rarely a catalyst for investors to buy or sell shares in the sector,” Rambourg writes. “Instead, it is more a function of sales momentum, which we see picking up soon.” The industry has faced multiple challenges. China’s ongoing property slump, US tariffs in 2025, jittery equity markets, upcoming midterm elections and higher rates, as well as the ongoing Middle East conflict and other geopolitical tensions have weighed on spending decisions. “There have been many reasons for consumers to cancel or delay purchases of discretionary products,” Rambourg writes. Still, these broader factors probably haven’t been the main constraint, he says, attributing the weak performance in recent years mostly to “a degree of strategic inertia” among luxury brands. Price hikes after the Covid pandemic, which were perceived as excessive by some observers, likely played a larger role in the slowdown in growth for luxury goods. More affordable luxury brands benefited as traditional high-end names hiked prices—estimated at around 60% between mid-2019 and mid-2026—opening space in the market that they could fill, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “As a direct impact of elevated price points and a value proposition that became less compelling across many brands, it appears that many target consumers decided to pass on purchasing luxury goods,” Rambourg writes. Alongside the aggressive price increases, limited innovation by the industry in the post-Covid period led to diminished consumer interest, and store traffic tailed off. That said, a number of luxury companies have new CEOs and creative directors who started presenting their collections last year. “We believe that it likely takes three to four collections for consumers to recognize—and possibly buy into—the change,” Rambourg writes. For many years there has been “a surprising disconnect between wealth in the US (high) and luxury demand among American consumers (low),” Rambourg points out. The market was likely restrained by a “guilt factor” or by “outlet culture,” he says. However, behaviors have begun to change since the Covid pandemic. “The appetite of American consumers for luxury goods has picked up strongly,” he writes. Luxury brands have taken notice, and store openings are multiplying. “While it may sound counterintuitive, we still think the US is an emerging market for luxury goods,” he adds. Elsewhere in the world, South Korean demand growth may be somewhat fragile because it is linked to wealth in the country’s tech-heavy and volatile equity market. The importance of Hong Kong for luxury brands has diminished over time, but the market is showing signs of recovery, with both local consumers and visitors from mainland China supporting sales growth, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The luxury goods companies Goldman Sachs Research covers have recorded average top-line growth of 6% annually over the past 25 years. “While growth has been pedestrian of late,” sales levels exceed what a 6% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) would have implied since just before the Covid pandemic in 2019, Rambourg points out. “In other words, the bear argument that the sector may have gone ex-growth for an extended period is not one we agree with,” he writes. To help understand where the sector and individual luxury goods makers may be headed, the report includes a benchmarking framework. This provides a way to think about long-term growth drivers, broken down as seven Cs. One of the Cs is clout, and Rambourg posits that “big is beautiful” in the luxury sector. He notes that bigger brands not only tend to secure better locations, but they also benefit from lower rent as a percentage of sales. Another is categories, with some consumer verticals, such as jewelry, having better growth potential than others, such as beauty products. Other considerations in the framework include: consumer caliber, referencing the relative resilience of high-net-worth consumers, which can likewise make high-end brands more resilient; and creativity, which may be difficult for equity analysts to quantify but does come into play in assessing prospects for luxury companies. Rounding out the list are consistency, which gets to the clarity of brand positioning; codes and icons, which are not necessarily loud logos but can be a discreet symbol, pattern, or logo only identifiable by people who know the products well; and finally, corporate considerations, as many luxury-goods companies are partly owned and run by family members. title: Birdie G’s Finds Its Next Chapter at Fairmont Century Plaza - Locale Magazine
content:
Birdie G’s, the beloved concept from James Beard-nominated Chef Jeremy Fox, officially opens at Fairmont Century Plaza on Oct. 26, ushering in a dynamic new culinary chapter at the property. Reimagined as an expansive American brasserie serving breakfast, lunch and dinner, the new Birdie G’s brings its signature creativity and spirit to Century City. Named for Fox’s daughter Birdie and his grandmother Gladys, Birdie G’s is known for its nostalgic yet inventive approach to American comfort cuisine rooted in family tradition, regional flavors and meticulous craftsmanship. Fox is a Food & Wine Best New Chef and a widely respected voice in California’s produce-driven cooking movement, and he originally opened the restaurant in 2019 at Bergamot Station. Born in Cleveland and raised across the Midwest and Deep South before settling in California, he draws on his personal journey, regional foodways and childhood memories of family meals and classic chain restaurants to craft a thoughtful and fun dining experience. At Fairmont Century Plaza, Birdie G’s evolves into an inviting neighborhood institution that honors the timeless spirit of classic Midwest supper clubs, where comfort, effortless polish and welcoming ease converge. Designed in partnership with EDG Design, the airy, light-filled space combines 1970s revival and midcentury sophistication with warmth and lived-in comfort. Comfy banquettes pair with warm rust and brown tones, custom leather touches and clean lines. The custom green plaid barstools are a playful nod to the exact interior of Fox’s original 1969 VW Beetle. The result is a fun, relaxed atmosphere that blends family traditions with Midwest Nice and Southern Hospitality. “In a lot of ways, this is more Birdie G’s than the original Birdie G’s,” Fox says. “The look and feel we always imagined never quite came together the first time, and here it finally has. You walk out of this sleek, modern lobby and step back in time into your grandparents’ rumpus room, with knick-knacks on the walls and all the little details that tell the story of where this food comes from. It’s the kind of place you have to experience in person, and I can’t wait to welcome everyone in to see it for themselves.” The menu features timeless American dishes transformed by Fox’s innovative techniques, handcrafted production and commitment to local, sustainable ingredients from regional farmers, ranchers and artisans. Breakfast features comforting morning classics with subtle deli and diner undertones. The Smoked Fish Platter comes with a bagel, cucumber, cherry tomato, pickled onion, roe, capers, crème fraîche, chives and dill. The Cornbread Waffle arrives with sweet pepper jam and popcorn butter, and the Brûléed French Toast is topped with spiced apple, Spanish peanuts and smoked cinnamon chantilly. For something heartier, Steak & Eggs pairs a koji-marinated hanger steak with two eggs any style, breakfast potatoes and three peppercorn sauce. Lunch can be friendly and casual or an elevated executive experience for the Century City business crowd. Crisp seasonal salads include The Century Plaza Wedge with little gems, smoked bacon, deviled egg mousse, cherry tomato, red onion, scallion and Bay Blue cheese. There’s also a Chopped Antipasto Salad that can be topped with salmon, hanger steak or chicken breast. Signature entrees include the Birdie Burger & Fries with onion jam, shaved onion, Cooper sharp cheddar and AL’s steak sauce, along with a Croque Madame and the Corned Beef Tongue Reuben. Both lunch and dinner feature The Pickle Chick, a gluten-free schnitzel with cucumber, cornichon, whipped feta, dill pickle sauce, horseradish and dill pollen. Both menus also offer Prime Steak Frites made with prime Flannery beef grilled with a Montreal rub and served with fries and aioli. Cuts include an 8-ounce hanger, a 12-ounce New York strip and a 28-ounce bone-in Jorge Ribeye dry-aged for 28 days. Each comes with your choice of sauce, including AL’ Steak Sauce, Horsey Cream, Pot Roast Butter and Three Peppercorn. The evening menu highlights generous portions and elegant cuts of steaks and chops, poultry and seafood. The Lamb a la Saless features a fat-capped lamb saddle marinated in fenugreek, black lime and beet molasses, served with crispy dill rice, dates and saffron yogurt. Mt. Lassen Trout comes with potato, smoked trout roe sauce and chive, and Chicken & Vegetables From the Rotisserie is served with root stoemp, cabbage, schmaltz, gribenes and beurre poulet. Inventive vegetable dishes include Sprouting Broccoli with miso bagna cauda and hippy seed mix. The Fioretto Cauliflower Kugel is a casserole of duck egg noodles baked with four-cheese mornay, garlic confit and bread crumbs. Fan favorites make an appearance too, like Fresh Cucumbers pickled to order in dill pickle sauce and Matzo Ball Soup served with one golden spoon. To start, there’s Bub & Grandma’s Bread or Five-Onion Dip & Potato Chips, which can be topped with N25 caviar. The menu pays homage to Fox’s culinary journey with an extra touch of hospitality: here, a Birdie’s dozen means 14. The restaurant’s iconic desserts remain an essential part of the menu. The World-Famous Rose Petal Pie is a terrazzo of raspberry, hibiscus and strawberry gelées in rosewater cream with a buttered pretzel crust. It’s joined by the nostalgic Malted Chocolate Layer Cake and the Sticky Date Bundt Cake with salted caramel sauce, because nobody has ever complained about too much caramel. The Creamsicle Rice Pudding comes with market citrus, coconut milk, preserved lemon and orange blossom, and at dinner, look for the Sugar Cream Tart, which the menu describes as crème brûlée in a pie crust. Since the restaurant is named for Fox’s daughter, young diners are treated with equal reverence. The dedicated kids menu offers thoughtfully made Potato-Crusted Chicken Fingers, pasta, Matzo Pizza Margherita and the playful Healthy Yucky Green Salad. The bar program leans into farmers market produce and a variety of housemade infused spirits, syrups and tinctures. The cocktail menu serves nostalgic classics alongside modern creations. Morning sips include a Bloody Mary made with the restaurant’s signature mix and Hibiscus Heat with lime, agave, citrus, tequila blanco and habanero. There’s also Spritzing in Sunny Century City with Carpano Bianco, Mommenpop blood orange and sparkling wine. The wine list ranges from global classic vintages to unique selections from winemakers dedicated to soil health. Birdie G’s is open daily, with coffee starting at 6 a.m. Breakfast and lunch are served from 6:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., and dinner runs from 5:30 to 9 p.m. Reservations are available on OpenTable. For private events, email events@birdiegsla.com. Celebrating its 60th anniversary in 2026, Fairmont Century Plaza stands as a reimagined icon following a $2.5 billion renovation. The property features 400 expansive guest rooms with private terraces, 63 luxury residences and the 14,000-square-foot Fairmont Spa Century Plaza. It also offers 24,000 square feet of private event space, including one of the largest ballrooms in Los Angeles. The hotel was originally built in 1966 on the site of a former 20th Century Fox Studios backlot. It has hosted legendary moments, from the Beatles winning big at the 10th Annual Grammy Awards to the Presidential State Dinner hosted by President Nixon to honor the Apollo 11 astronauts. Birdie G’s officially opens Oct. 26 at Fairmont Century Plaza, located at 2025 Ave of the Stars in Century City. There’s also the Creamsicle Rice Pudding for dessert, which is vegan and gluten-free as well. Yes. title: 310-HP V6, AWD, Torque Vectoring - Buick's Final Sports Sedan Costs Half As Much As A New Golf R - CarBuzz
content: We added a section with one more powerful luxury sedan that's worth around $20k on the used market. If there's one thing that we gearheads can agree on, it's that new car prices are ridiculous. In fact, the average price for a new car in the US has hit $50,000. That's almost exactly the price of a new  Volkswagen Golf R, and while it may be fast, safe, and comfortable, what if your money were best spent on something used? Something a bit more practical with similar performance, perhaps? Enter: the Buick Regal GS. This American sports sedan was more than a rebadged European family car, offering performance and space without the high price tag. You can now easily find this car for less than half the price of a used Golf R – something we still can't quite understand. Here's why... Buick knew that time was running out for its sedans in the 2010s. The automaker's SUV sales were surging, and while the fifth-gen Regal sedan was a great car, its looks were becoming outdated and customers started looking elsewhere. That's why in 2017, the sixth-generation Regal debuted with a much more handsome exterior and interior. The writing was on the wall for this car, which is why Buick decided to go out with a bang. The GS trim was introduced as the halo version, featuring a larger 3.6L V6 engine and sportier cosmetics. While we think of ultra-exclusive Italian supercars as collectibles, the Regal GS's low production number of around 1,300 means it's exclusive and represents perhaps the last true performance-oriented Buick like this. For the company that gave us the GNX and Skylark GS, it's safe to say that collectors love the last-of-the-line model.But nostalgia alone doesn't justify a purchase – so what does the GS actually deliver behind the wheel? The GS badge meant the Regal was ready to be driven hard. Its 3.6L V6 engine has strong links to the Chevrolet Colorado and GMC Canyon of the same vintage, but here it makes 310 horsepower and 282 lb-ft through a clever all-wheel-drive system. That AWD system isn't old-fashioned, either, as it has torque vectoring capabilities that mean it can send up to 100% of the engine's power to an individual rear wheel through two computer-controlled clutches. This AWD system is also used in the TourX wagon, but in the GS driving mode, it will send more of its power to the rear wheels. This driving mode also firms up the adaptive suspension, quickens throttle response, makes the steering heavier, and lets the nine-speed automatic hold onto gears longer. It's exactly what you want in a sports sedan – the ability to be comfortable in most situations and then turn into a sports car when asked. Beyond the engine and AWD system, there's a lot to love. The transmission is smooth, it can reach 60 miles per hour in under six seconds, and reaches a top speed of 167 miles per hour. The GS' Brembo brakes are also solid. Without turbochargers, the V6 produces linear power that you'll want to unleash. It makes peak torque at 5,200 rpm and peak power at 6,800 rpm, meaning it has that old-school rev-happy character. So, it's half the price of a new Golf R – is it half the amount of fun? Definitely not. The V6 in the GS makes only 18 hp and 13 lb-ft of torque less than Volkswagen's 2.0L turbo-four, and while it may be a second slower to 60 miles per hour, it offers much of the same on-paper performance. Of course, the Golf R's 4Motion all-wheel-drive system is much more modern and advanced, leading to super-grippy all-weather performance, but the Buick isn't far behind. The Regal's performance means it's easily faster than the Golf GTI, and while the modern hot hatches may be more agile, the Buick's slightly longer wheelbase may make it more stable at speed. Volkswagen offers the Golf R with standard adaptive suspension, meaning just like the Regal, it's a superb daily driver but turns into a monster when asked. The best thing about both the Regal GS and the Golf R is how they combine performance and everyday usability. This stretches to the design, as the GS badges on the Buick are subdued and, unless you were looking, you wouldn't be able to tell it's the flagship. The Golf looks a bit racier with its spoiler and vents, especially in a bright color that complements its stance. We love the design of both, but those wanting a sleeper will prefer the GS. Even with the younger Golf in comparison, the Buick Regal GS isn't as sparse as you may think. There's ventilated seating, keyless start, and most impressively, massage controls for both front seats. Of course, the Golf has the larger infotainment display, as that's where the industry is heading, but the GS has smartphone connectivity so you're not stuck with an outdated system. The only thing that we can see the Golf having over the Regal is rear heated seats and a better sound system. It's worth mentioning size, too, as the Buick wins easily here. The Golf manages just under 20 cubic feet of space in the cargo bay, while the GS can manage 31.5 cubes. It also has more rear legroom at 36.9 inches compared to 35 inches, and its hatchback design makes it highly practical. With only 1,300 units made, the Buick Regal GS isn't super common on the marketplace, so when one pops up, we'd certainly be reaching out quickly. You won't have to worry about high-mileage examples, either, as the LGX family of 3.6L V6 engines is said to be reliable when properly maintained. It's an improvement over previous GM blocks like this. Very high-mileage examples may benefit from a cleanup around the intake valves, which can clog with carbon buildup. Some owners also recommend getting the timing chain checked out, so a recent service stamp for this is ideal. Given its status as a sports sedan, make sure you're getting a well-cared-for example with service history. At the time of writing, we can see listings range from $20–$25k for cars with around 60,000 miles. You can dip under $20k if you go for listings with around 100,000 miles, and we wouldn't be worried about reliability with its decent record. Even if you find an unreliable example, you'll still be way under the Golf R's price with some repairs and servicing. Can you feel the 18 hp difference between these two cars by the seat of your pants? Probably not. The Regal GS is a more practical sleeper sedan that has just as many creature comforts as the Golf, without the intrusive new-car chimes and alerts. And for half the price, you can't go wrong. On the topic of affordable, luxurious, powerful sedans, we can't help but bring up the 2017–2020 Lincoln MKZ. It's technically built on the same boring platform as the Ford Fusion, but the MKZ's top trim level, the Reserve, was powered by the same engine found under the Ford Bronco Raptor's hood today. Drivers can enjoy a 3.0-liter twin-turbo V6 that makes 350 horsepower when paired with a front-wheel-drive drivetrain, or 400 horsepower with all-wheel drive. Flooring it from a stop sign results in a 4.8-second 0-60 mph sprint on its way to a 150 mph limited top speed. The best part of it all is that buyers can find a 2020 MKZ Reserve for around $20,000 today in average condition. Some low-mileage examples are listed for $25k or slightly higher, but most buyers can find good examples for cheaper. Browse local listings, compare prices, and find the right car for you. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. Unfortunately, too few were built—which is certainly not good for us fans. Why were there so few variants of this final generation of the Buick Regal? Along with the Buick Regal TourX, there was clear customer demand for the Buick Regal GS; however, at that time, GM sold the Opel brand to PSA. PSA decided that only a limited number of Opel vehicles based on the GM architecture could continue to be produced. That is why production at the Opel plant in Rüsselsheim, Germany, came to an end! Furthermore, the base vehicle—the Opel Insignia B—was also manufactured as a Vauxhall and a Holden. So, in total, the production numbers were actually quite high! With this move, GM has exited the sedan and wagon market globally! Cadillac now produces only two sedan models, and even those are slated to be discontinued by 2026. In doing so, they are effectively handing over a key customer base to other brands—brands that Buick and Cadillac customers likely never wanted in the first place. The manufacturers that still produce sedans—and, in some cases, coupes, convertibles, or uninspired wagons—include BMW, Mercedes, Audi, Toyota, and Mazda. The Zacks rating relies solely on a company's changing earnings picture. The power of a changing earnings picture in determining near-term stock price movements makes the Zacks rating system highly useful for individual investors, since it can be difficult to make decisions based on rating upgrades by Wall Street analysts. These are mostly driven by subjective factors that are hard to see and measure in real time. The change in a company's future earnings potential, as reflected in earnings estimate revisions, and the near-term price movement of its stock are proven to be strongly correlated. That's partly because of the influence of institutional investors that use earnings and earnings estimates for calculating the fair value of a company's shares. An increase or decrease in earnings estimates in their valuation models simply results in higher or lower fair value for a stock, and institutional investors typically buy or sell it. title: Men’s Giant Slalom preview: Odermatt & Pinheiro Braathen prepare to resume battle as challengers gather - FIS Ski
content: It may only be the first race of a new season but it already feels like there is so much riding on the men’s Audi FIS World Cup Giant Slalom in Sölden on Sunday. Will newly crowned Olympic and World Cup champion Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) continue his golden form and kickstart a tilt at this season’s Overall title? Might the equally in-form Loic Meillard (SUI/Rossignol) finally conquer the infamous Rettenbach Glacier and lay down a marker of his own? Which of the quartet of impressive Norwegians will emerge strongest? Can a Marco Schwarz (AUT/Atomic) free of Slalom considerations become Austria’s first winner of the home opener in 12 years? Is everyone mad to even countenance anything but another GS masterclass from Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli)? All these questions, and more, will be answered when the action gets underway with the first run at 10:00 CET. For four seasons, 2022-2025, no one could get near Odermatt on GS skis. The Swiss megastar not only claimed a quartet of Crystal Globes, he did it in truly dominant style. The zenith came in 2023/24 when only a second run DNF in the World Cup Finals in Saalbach prevented Odi from completing an extraordinary season sweep. Two wins in the first three races last season suggested more of the same. But no one had told Pinheiro Braathen. From late December through to the final race in Lillehammer, the Brazilian went on a tear. A run of finishes that read 2nd-2nd-2nd-1st-1st propelled him up the GS standings and, thanks to that final-day victory when everything was on the line, past a bemused Odermatt. A first ever World Cup Globe for Brazil was accompanied by a first ever Olympic gold medal, with Pinheiro Braathen once again relegating the great Odermatt to second place. The challenge has well and truly been laid down. The sense of an epic rivalry only increased recently when Pinheiro Braathen made it clear he will add the Super G to his schedule in an attempt to also snatch Odi’s Overall crown. There is nowhere better than Sölden to kick it all off. While Odermatt is a master of the Rettenbach’s particular challenges and will chase a fourth win to tie Ted Ligety (USA) as the resort’s most successful male skier, Pinheiro Braathen has tasted success here too, winning in 2020. Not that the rest of a high quality field have any intention of letting the duo take over. GS world champion in 2019, GS Globe winner in 2020 and second in the standings in three of the past five seasons, Kristoffersen has all the attributes to muscle into the reckoning once more. “Until you beat (Ingemar) Stenmark on World Cup wins, I think there is always a goal to be had,” the 32-year-old said with a smile. “Of course, not every day is easy, but in the end the motivation is still there.” Part of a Norwegian clean sweep in Sölden two seasons ago and with another podium place in 2022, it would seem Kristoffersen knows how to get the most out of the early season stop. Even if the man himself is not entirely convinced. “The long step pitch is something special, and I’m not the best at stivoting, and I haven’t really cracked the code properly yet on how to do it turn after turn in Sölden. But we still keep on trying as best as we can,” he said, before adding, “Of course, there are hills which fit my style of skiing better.” There certainly are. Now happily on Head skis, Kristoffersen has won four World Cup GS races in Kranjska Gora and two in Alta Badia. Both are once more on the roster. Meillard is another with his eyes quietly on all sorts of prizes. The Swiss man has been electric over the past 18 months. Reigning Olympic and world Slalom champion, Meillard came mighty close to snatching last season’s GS World Cup Globe at the death. Add on the power of the nappy factor, and the 29-year-old is clearly one to watch. Meillard has finished in the top three in the GS Globe race in each of the past three seasons. A stat he almost matched in the Overall standings, with only a fourth-place finish last season dropping him off that podium. While Odermatt’s superb form in both the Downhill and Super G, alongside the GS, give him a clear advantage in the hunt for the Big Globe, his compatriot does have a chance to challenge him there too. “Tough to follow all three disciplines, be home, train, rest correctly, so, the focus at the beginning will be on Slalom and GS and then we will see as the season goes,” Meillard revealed in Sölden. “Definitely keeping it (the Super G) in my training (schedule) it definitely helps with GS to have that speed, and to be a bit more patient.” In somewhat of a contrast, it will be fascinating to see how Schwarz goes in Sölden, now that he has reduced his packed schedule from four disciplines to three. The 2021 Alpine combined world champion has dropped the Slalom, after three wins and 14 podium places in 105 World Cup starts. Sölden is not a bad place for his new adventure to start. Last year Schwarz became the first home hope to end on the podium in four years, and with a win following in Alta Badia, the Austrian clearly has the skills and confidence to challenge again. Fellow local, Stefan Brennsteiner (AUT/Fischer) is also in fine form. In fact, the 35-year-old has never been better. A win and six further top-five finishes propelled him to fourth in the GS standings last time out, his best ever finish in 11 seasons on tour. At the other end of the age scale, Alexander Steen Olsen’s (NOR/Rossignol) return to the starting line-up is a very welcome sight. The last time the 25-year-old competed in Sölden he won. A knee injury then kept the youngster out for the entirety of last season but he is now fit and firing once more. The battle for supremacy within the Attacking Vikings will be almost as fascinating as their efforts to top the rest of the field. Atle Lie McGrath (NOR/Head) finished off a wild season last time out with a brilliant Slalom Globe. The 26-year-old is yet to win a GS World Cup race, but he does have five podiums to his name, two of them coming in Sölden in the past two seasons. Timon Haugan (NOR/Van Deer) cannot yet match that GS consistency but he did finish last season with four top-five finishes in his final six races. Big names doing great things everywhere you look. Do not miss the start of the GS season, 10:00 CET Sunday.
